writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only bidirectional-bfs program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
The ladder hit→hot→dot→dog→cog contains 5 words and 4 transformations. Search from both endpoints and expand the smaller frontier layer, comparing meeting distances. No valid connecting sequence yields the explicit result 0.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Return word-ladder length changing one letter at a time. The visible fixture is `hit -> cog via [hot,dot,dog,lot,log,cog]` and its example result is `5`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Bidirectional BFS when it asks for unweighted shortest paths with one source and one target. Here the concrete task is: Return word-ladder length changing one letter at a time. The visible input `hit -> cog via [hot,dot,dog,lot,log,cog]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Inspect weight signs and graph direction: non-negative shortest paths, negative edges, and zero-one weights support different algorithms. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Expand the smaller frontier from each endpoint until the visited sets meet. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? Edge weights change what a path means. State whether the objective is minimum distance, a spanning structure, or feasible flow before choosing state. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(b^(d/2)) frontier typical · O(V) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `5` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Check disconnected vertices, parallel edges, zero weights, and whether an unreachable result has a defined representation. Use numeric types wide enough for distances, weights, or capacities. In shortest-path heap variants, skip stale queue entries and guard sentinel arithmetic. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
